# Santorini Catamaran Cruises: Which Type Should You Actually Book?

**Short answer:** choose a daytime cruise if swimming matters more than sunset, a small-group cruise if you want a good balance of space and price, and a private catamaran if you care most about privacy, flexibility or controlling the atmosphere.

The word **“luxury”** tells you surprisingly little.

A much better way to choose is to look at four things: **how many people will actually be on board, when the cruise sails, how much swimming time you get, and how much control you want over the day.**

Those differences can turn two almost identical-looking Santorini catamarans into completely different experiences.

## Start with the kind of day you actually want

A Santorini catamaran cruise is usually sold with the same photographs: white boat, blue water, volcanic cliffs, glasses of wine and somebody jumping into the sea.

But there are really several different products hiding behind those pictures.

**Daytime** makes the most sense if swimming, snorkeling and being in the water are your priorities.

**Sunset** makes more sense if the atmosphere of the evening matters as much as swimming.

**Small-group** is the middle ground: you share the boat, but avoid the feeling of being one passenger among fifty.

**Private** is not simply the expensive version. It is the version where the group, pace and atmosphere belong to you.

That distinction is more useful than asking which Santorini catamaran is “best”.

## How many people are really on board?

This is the first number I would check.

“Small group” is not a standardized term.

One current sunset catamaran limits the boat to **13 passengers**.

Another popular premium small-group cruise allows up to **20**.

A much larger shared catamaran currently allows up to **55 passengers**.

All three are sold as Santorini catamaran experiences.

They are not the same experience.

Thirteen people can spread around the deck without constantly negotiating space.

Twenty is still reasonably intimate on a good-sized catamaran, but you will notice the group.

Fifty-five becomes a much more social cruise. That may be exactly what you want if you enjoy meeting people, music and a livelier atmosphere.

But if your mental picture involves quietly stretching out on the netting with a glass of wine, maximum passenger count matters more than the word **premium** in the title.

## If I wanted a very small sunset group

One current option stands out because it caps the group at **13 travellers**.

It lasts about five hours and includes hotel pickup, a Greek BBQ meal, white wine and soft drinks, snorkeling equipment, towels and Wi-Fi.

The itinerary includes swimming stops around the caldera and finishes with sunset views beneath the cliffs of Oia.

That is the format I would look at for a couple who wants the classic Santorini sunset without immediately jumping to the price of a private charter.

[Santorini Sunset Luxury Sailing Catamaran Cruise with BBQ, drinks, transfer](https://www.viator.com/tours/Santorini/Santorini-Lagoon-560-Sunset-Tour-with-BBQ-and-Drinks/d959-7207P3?pid=P00320497&mcid=42383&medium=link&medium_version=selector "affiliate-button")

The important reason to choose it is not that it has a prettier boat.

It is the passenger limit.

## Daytime vs sunset is not simply “same cruise, prettier ending”

Sunset sounds automatically better.

It is not necessarily better for everyone.

If swimming is your main reason for booking, I would seriously consider the daytime departure.

You are on the water when the sun is high, swimming feels like the centre of the day rather than something before the main sunset event, and you are not spending the final part of the cruise waiting for the light to change.

Sunset cruises have a different rhythm.

There is usually swimming first, then food, sailing and the gradual shift toward the evening.

You also need to remember that the Aegean can feel surprisingly cool once the sun disappears. Recent passengers regularly mention being glad they had a light jacket or the blankets supplied onboard.

And one detail is easy to misunderstand:

**not every sunset cruise watches the sunset from Oia.**

Some sail below Oia.

Some watch it from another part of the caldera or open water.

Some follow the daytime itinerary in reverse.

If the exact sunset location matters to you, read the itinerary rather than assuming that “Santorini sunset cruise” means “sunset beneath Oia”.

## The 20-person sweet spot

For many people, I think around twenty passengers is the sensible compromise.

One of the strongest examples is the Spiridakos premium small-group cruise.

It currently runs for about five hours with a maximum of **20 travellers**.

Pickup and drop-off are included, as are snorkeling equipment, towels, a substantial BBQ meal, soft drinks, beer, white wine and cocktails.

Recent travellers describe plenty of swimming time and enough space to spread out once everyone settles on the boat.

This is the kind of option I would compare first if I wanted the full Santorini catamaran experience without either paying for private or sharing with fifty people.



[Luxury Small-Group Catamaran Cruise with BBQ, Open bar & Transfer](https://www.viator.com/tours/Santorini/Santorini-Sailing-Cruise-by-Luxury-Catamaran-with-BBQ-and-Drinks/d959-17549P13?pid=P00320497&mcid=42383&medium=link&medium_version=selector "affiliate-button")

One caveat is worth knowing: the operator states that the starting or ending port and itinerary can change because of weather or operational conditions.

That is not necessarily a problem.

On an island, sometimes it is simply seamanship.

But it is something to know before you build the rest of your day around a specific port.

## What does the price actually include?

This is another place where comparing headline prices can mislead you.

Many Santorini cruises include much more than the boat itself.

The better shared packages commonly include transfers, food, soft drinks, wine or beer, snorkeling equipment and towels.

Some add cocktails or Wi-Fi.

But read the details carefully.

“Hotel pickup” may not mean somebody stops outside your hotel door.

Many properties in Oia, Fira, Imerovigli and other steep or pedestrian areas cannot be reached by minibus.

The Spiridakos listing, for example, explains that your pickup location may be a short walk from your accommodation.

That is a small distinction when you are travelling light.

It feels less small when you have children, mobility issues or are standing in the sun wondering where the minibus is.

## Booking trap #1: the hot springs are not a spa

“Swim in the Santorini hot springs” sounds wonderful.

It also creates the wrong mental picture.

You are not stepping from the catamaran into a steaming natural pool.

On some cruises, the catamaran stays around **50 metres away** from the warmer, yellowish water and passengers swim toward it.

The operator of one large shared cruise says the hot-spring water may be only up to about **4°C warmer** than the surrounding clear sea.

So if you do not swim confidently, do not choose the cruise because the words “hot springs” sound relaxing.

Ask how the stop actually works.

## Booking trap #2: your port may not be the port you imagined

Vlychada, Ammoudi and other points around Santorini appear across different itineraries.

Weather and operational conditions can also affect where a cruise begins or ends.

Do not plan a restaurant reservation fifteen minutes after the advertised arrival time at the opposite end of the island.

The cruise may be five hours.

The complete experience — pickup, collecting other passengers, sailing and returning everyone afterward — can consume noticeably more of your day.

A recent passenger on a small-group cruise reported spending a long time in the return shuttle because several people had to be dropped around the island.

That does not make the cruise bad.

It is simply part of the logistics that the glossy deck photographs do not show.

## Booking trap #3: free cancellation does not mean the route is guaranteed

The current cruises I checked generally offer cancellation up to 24 hours beforehand for a full refund.

That is useful.

But a confirmed booking does not freeze the sea.

Wind and weather can affect sailing routes, swimming stops, departure points and timing.

If one specific stop is the entire reason you are booking, check how the operator handles route changes.

A responsible skipper may change the plan.

That is preferable to forcing the advertised itinerary in poor conditions.

## What about the big 55-passenger cruises?

I would not automatically reject them.

One current Ocean Voyager product allows up to **55 travellers**, includes food, drinks, pickup and swimming stops, and has plenty of enthusiastic reviews.

For someone travelling with friends who wants a social atmosphere, it may make perfect sense.

It can also cost substantially less than very-small-group or private alternatives.

But this is exactly why I do not like generic articles called **“Best Santorini Catamaran Cruises.”**

The same boat can be “best” for one traveller and completely wrong for another.

If I were travelling as a couple looking for quiet, I would pay more for fewer people.

If I were travelling with a group of friends who wanted music, drinks and other people around, fifty passengers would bother me much less.

## When private becomes worth the money

Private is where the calculation changes completely.

One current private full-day catamaran lasts about seven hours and is available only to your group.

It includes a private crew, meals, open bar, snorkeling equipment and transfers.

The itinerary can cover a much larger part of Santorini, including the caldera, Thirassia and the area below Oia.

The point is not simply that nobody else is there.

You gain control over the rhythm of the day.

Want longer in the water?

Want less time somewhere else?

Want privacy as a couple?

Travelling with children?

Celebrating something?

Do not want your expensive sunset determined by the personality of twenty strangers?

Those are much better reasons for booking private than simply wanting the most expensive option.



[Santorini Full Day Catamaran Private Cruise incl. Meal, Drinks & Free Transport](https://www.viator.com/tours/Santorini/Santorini-Catamaran-TailorMade-Private-Full-Day-Cruise/d959-63718P6?pid=P00320497&mcid=42383&medium=link&medium_version=selector "affiliate-button")

It is expensive.

I would not pretend otherwise.

But if four, six or eight people are already travelling together, I would at least compare the total private price with buying that many individual places on a premium shared cruise.

Sometimes the difference looks different when you calculate it per group rather than per person.

## Which would I choose?

For **a couple on a first Santorini trip**, I would probably choose the 13-person sunset cruise.

It preserves the sunset experience without paying private-charter money.

For **a family**, I would lean toward a 20-person daytime small-group cruise or private, depending on budget. Daytime keeps the day centred on swimming rather than stretching toward a late sunset.

For **friends who enjoy a social atmosphere**, I would not automatically pay to reduce the group from 55 to 13. A larger shared cruise may actually suit the mood better.

For **someone who mainly wants to swim**, I would choose daytime before sunset and look closely at actual swim-stop duration.

And for **a honeymoon, proposal, anniversary or someone who simply values control**, I would look at private.

Not because private is inherently “better”.

Because control is what you are paying for.

## Dan's recommendation

I have not taken these particular cruises myself.

I compared the current itineraries, passenger limits, inclusions, booking conditions and recent traveller reports because the Santorini catamaran market makes very different products look almost identical.

My first filter would be passenger count.

Then daytime versus sunset.

Then I would ask how much of the five hours is actually swimming and relaxing rather than transfer logistics.

Only after that would I compare price.

For most first-time visitors, I think a genuinely small shared catamaran is the sweet spot.

You get the caldera, swimming, food and the absurd pleasure of watching Santorini from the water without paying for an entire boat.

But if privacy or atmosphere matters enough that the wrong group could spoil the day, I would stop trying to optimize the shared option and look at private.

The simplest rule is probably this:

**Do not book the word “luxury”.**

**Book the kind of day you actually want.**

## Before you book

Check the maximum number of passengers, exact departure type, pickup location, swim stops and cancellation policy on the current listing.

Then ask yourself one last question:

**Would I still be happy with this cruise if the sunset were cloudy?**

If the answer is yes because you like the boat, swimming, food and time at sea, you have probably chosen well.

If the entire value depends on one perfect orange photograph beneath Oia, I would think again.
